context_blurb:
A rattlesnake in ambush, a lizard on a sunny rock, a fish in seawater below freezing: each survives by adaptations, inherited traits that help a living thing survive and raise young where it lives. Natural selection spreads them, for animals whose traits suit their home leave more young.

Adaptations come in three kinds: structural, part of the body's build, such as its shape, fur or colouring; behavioural, something the animal does; and physiological, an inner working of the body, such as its chemistry or the way an organ does its job.

A desert rattlesnake shows all three. Its blotchy scales hide it against the ground, part of its build; its venom is a chemical made in its venom glands; and lying motionless in ambush is something it does. So its colouring, venom and ambush are structural, physiological and behavioural, in that order.

Kangaroo rats, desert rodents, waste little water, for their kidneys make urine some five times more concentrated than human kidneys can. The kidneys are body parts, but the adaptation is the way the organ works, so it is physiological.

Lizards were long called cold-blooded, as if they were simply as warm as the air. But in 1944, after four years in the California desert, Raymond Cowles and Charles Bogert showed that active lizards hold their bodies near a favourite temperature by behaviour, basking when cool and slipping into shade when hot. A mouse makes its warmth inside, a physiological way, by burning food day and night. The lizard burns little food to keep warm, so it lives on ten to twenty times less food than a mammal its size.

In 1961 Arthur DeVries, a graduate student, went to Antarctica to study fish in seawater nearly two degrees Celsius below zero, a cold that would freeze an ordinary fish's blood. He and Donald Wohlschlag found that dissolved salts did only about half the job; a protein studded with sugars, an antifreeze, did much of the rest. Ice crystals get in with food and through the gills, and the antifreeze binds to tiny crystals so they cannot grow, keeping the blood liquid below its normal freezing point. This inner chemistry is a physiological adaptation.

Such traits begin as chance mutations, changes in genes that some animals inherit. Rock pocket mice of the Southwest are mostly sandy like the desert rock, but on dark lava nearly all are black, since owls that hunt by sight pick off pale mice there. Hopi Hoekstra and Michael Nachman found that black mice on one flow owe their coats to changes in a single coat-colour gene, while black mice on a flow hundreds of miles off inherit theirs through other genes. Two genetic routes to one coat mean that black coats arose separately on the two flows. Mutations happen by chance, but selection does not: the same dark rock favoured black coats twice.

For nearly eleven years Henry Walter Bates collected insects in the Amazon, where birds left alone some boldly marked, foul-tasting butterflies. He found rare look-alikes from an unrelated family that were good to eat: mimics, harmless copies of a harmful kind. Birds learn to shun the pattern by tasting foul ones. Were the mimics far commoner than the foul kind, birds would mostly find a meal behind the pattern and learn to hunt it, so this mimicry works only while the mimics stay rare.

Harmless scarlet kingsnakes copy the red, yellow and black rings of the venomous coral snake. David Pfennig's team laid hundreds of soft plasticine snakes, ringed, striped or plain brown, across the Carolinas, inside the coral snake's range and north of it. Bite marks in the clay showed that inside the range only about 6 percent of attacks fell on ringed models, but farther north, with no coral snakes, about half did. So the rings protect only where coral snakes live, because only there have hunters learned to fear the real thing.

John Endler tested guppies, small fish of Trinidad's mountain streams. He moved some from a stream where the fierce pike cichlid eats showy males to a stretch whose only other fish was a small killifish, a feeble hunter. Within about two years, some fifteen generations, the males there had bigger, brighter spots. Choosy female guppies prefer colourful males as mates, so once no pike cichlid picked off the showiest, the brightest males won the most mates and fathered the most young.
